label: A Discord voice channel for work

meta.title: Discord for Work: Is a Voice Channel Enough for a Remote Team?
meta.description: Why remote teams sit in a Discord voice channel all day, what Discord's own limits mean for a working team, and when a virtual office fits better.

title: Running your team's day in a Discord voice channel? What works, and what doesn't.
intro: Plenty of small remote teams spend the working day in a Discord voice channel: it's free, everyone can see who's in, and joining takes one click. It works well until the team needs two conversations at once, a place that's only for work, or more than a free server allows. Here is what Discord does well for a team, what its own documentation says about its limits, and when a virtual office fits better. We make TinyFloor, a virtual office, so we're not neutral; Discord's numbers are from Discord's own pages.
takeaways: A Discord voice channel gives a team something Slack and Zoom don't: you can see who's in and join with one click.
A voice channel holds one conversation. Talking to one person means both of you moving to another channel.
On a server without boosts, screen sharing is 720p at 30 frames a second, uploads are 10MB, and up to 25 people can be on video in a voice channel [1].
Discord has encrypted voice and video end to end since September 2024; text messages are not end-to-end encrypted [2].
Each person joins with their own Discord account, the same one they use for friends and games.

sections.title: Why do remote teams work in a Discord voice channel?
body: Because it gives them the thing Slack and Zoom leave out: being around each other. The server's sidebar shows who's in each voice channel, so you can see at a glance who's working, and joining them is one click with no link or invite.

It costs nothing, most people already have an account, the voice is fast, and screen sharing is built in. For a team of friends who started a company, or a team that came from gaming, it's the obvious place to start.

items.title: One conversation per channel
items.body: Everyone in a voice channel hears everyone. Two people who want to talk on their own both move to another channel, and the rest see them go. Teams end up with a channel for each kind of talk and people hopping between them.

items.title: Being in means being heard
items.body: By default your microphone is live in a voice channel unless you mute it or use push to talk, so most teams sit muted all day and unmute to speak, which makes starting a conversation feel like interrupting a room.

items.title: Work and personal life in one app
items.body: People bring their own Discord account, with their friends, their other servers and their notifications. Discord describes itself as a place to "deepen friendships around games and shared interests" [2].

items.title: Accounts belong to people, not the company
items.body: When someone leaves, you can remove them from the server, but the account, and any direct messages they had with the team, stay theirs.

items.title: Limits on a free server
items.body: Without boosts, uploads are capped at 10MB, streams at 720p and 30 frames a second, and video at 25 people per voice channel. Boosting the server raises uploads to 50MB at level 2 and 100MB at level 3 [1].

sections.title: What does Discord do better than a virtual office?

items.title: Price
items.body: A Discord server is free. A virtual office costs $5 to $20 a person a month, or one price for the whole office for a few; see [what a virtual office costs](/blog/virtual-office-cost).

items.title: Smooth screen sharing
items.body: Discord streams at 30 frames a second on a free server [1], which suits video and games. TinyFloor shares a screen at up to 720p and 10 to 15 frames a second, tuned for sharp text rather than motion [3].

items.title: Encryption
items.body: Discord's voice and video are end-to-end encrypted, in direct messages, group messages, voice channels and Go Live streams, under its DAVE protocol [2].

items.title: Apps everywhere
items.body: Discord has desktop and mobile apps that most people already have installed.

sections.title: What does a virtual office change?
body: A virtual office keeps the part that works, seeing who's in and joining without a link, and changes how conversations start.

items.title: Many conversations on one floor
items.body: The whole team is on one floor, and two people can talk while everyone else keeps working, without moving anywhere.

items.title: Nobody heard by accident
items.body: In TinyFloor you walk up to a teammate and start a call; nothing is heard until then, and a call starts with voice, with the camera a button [3]. Three or more meet in the meeting room.

items.title: A place that's only for work
items.body: People sign in with Google or a code sent to their email [3], and colleagues with the same work email domain can find the team's office and walk in, or ask to [4]. Nothing from anyone's personal life is in the room.

items.title: Desks and statuses
items.body: Each person has a desk and a status, so the floor shows who's focused and who's free, not only who's in a channel.

items.title: The team mostly talks as a group
items.body: If one open channel is how your team likes to work, and side conversations are rare, Discord does that for free.

items.title: Everyone already lives there
items.body: If the team uses Discord happily all day and mixing in personal servers isn't a problem, there's little reason to move.

items.title: It's time to move when
items.body: people hop between channels to talk in pairs, sit muted all day, mute the server to get away from other servers' noise, or a new hire has to make a Discord account just for work.

sections.title: Can a team use both?
body: Yes. Some teams keep a Discord server for their community or for after work, and move the working day to a virtual office. The two don't need to be connected.

faq.a: For a small team that likes talking as a group, it works and it's free. It gets harder when people need private conversations, when work and personal servers mix, or when the team outgrows a free server's limits: 10MB uploads, 720p screen sharing at 30 frames a second, and 25 people on video in a voice channel.

faq.q: Is Discord free for a team?
faq.a: Yes. A server and its voice channels are free. Server boosts raise the limits for everyone in the server, and Nitro raises them for one person.

Voice and video are end-to-end encrypted in direct messages, group messages, voice channels and Go Live streams, under the DAVE protocol Discord announced on 17 September 2024. Text messages are not end-to-end encrypted.

faq.q: How many people can be on video in a Discord voice channel?
faq.a: Up to 25 people with video, and up to 50 watching a Go Live stream, according to Discord's own list of limits.

faq.q: What's a good Discord alternative for a remote team?
faq.a: For writing, Slack. For the being-around-each-other part a Discord voice channel gives, a virtual office: the team on one floor, where two people can talk without moving channels.
